speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Singapore is a party to the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The Basel Convention is an international treaty governing the classification and transboundary movement of hazardous and other waste to protect human health and the environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The Basel Convention does not prohibit the transboundary movement of hazardous waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Instead, it controls the movement of hazardous waste via the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This is in recognition of the legitimate transboundary movements of hazardous waste as defined under the Convention, such as for proper recycling or disposal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Besides controlling hazardous waste, the Convention also imposes the PIC procedure on some non-hazardous waste streams, namely, household wastes and residues arising from the incineration of household wastes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: These waste streams are defined as "other waste" under the Basel Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Under the PIC procedure, exporting states that wish to export any waste stream that is covered by the Convention have to obtain prior consent from the countries receiving the waste, or the states of import, as well as the countries through which the waste transits, or the states of transit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Improper disposal of plastic waste has caused severe environmental pollution, adverse health effects and contributed to climate change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: As a responsible global citizen, Singapore joins the international community in supporting the amendments to the Basel Convention which will strengthen control of the transboundary movement of plastic waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: As a party to the Basel Convention, Singapore is required to implement domestic controls to regulate the transboundary movement of the covered categories of plastic waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Singapore fulfils our obligations to the Basel Convention through the Hazardous Waste (Control of Export, Import and Transit) Act (HWA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: HWA provides the legislative framework for the National Environment Agency (NEA) to ensure that Singapore complies with our obligations under the Basel Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This will enable us to meet our obligations arising from the amendments to the Basel Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: It also seeks to update NEA’s regulatory powers for more effective administration and enforcement of HWA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: I will start with the proposed amendments to include plastic waste within the scope of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Section 4 of HWA defines "hazardous waste" and "other waste" in accordance with the Basel Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The definition of "other waste" is currently based on the categories of waste listed under Annex II of the Basel Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: These are non-hazardous wastes that have to undergo the PIC procedure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The amendments to the Basel Convention will now expand Annex II to include certain categories of plastic waste which could impact the environment if not managed properly, such as mixed plastic waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clause 3 accordingly amends section 4 to define "other waste" as meaning waste belonging to any category under Annex II to the Basel Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The Schedule of HWA reproduces the texts and annexes of the Basel Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clause 7 amends the Schedule to include the categories of plastic waste covered by the amendments to the Basel Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: I will now highlight the amendments to facilitate the administration and enforcement of HWA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: HWA is currently administered by the Director of Hazardous Waste, as appointed by the Minister.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clauses 2, 5 and 8 make various amendments to HWA to make the Director-General of Environmental Protection, appointed under the Environmental Protection and Management Act (EPMA), responsible for the administration of HWA instead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: This is to align with the power of administration of other Acts under NEA, such as EPMA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Consequential amendments will be made to the Second Schedule of the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: The Basel Convention allows parties to lodge with its Secretariat the parties’ national definitions of "hazardous waste" and "other waste" beyond the scope of the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: These national definitions are published on the official Basel Convention website.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Section 5 of HWA allows the Minister, through notification in the Gazette, to extend the definition of “hazardous waste” or “other waste” in the Act to include these national definitions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Clause 4 adds a new subsection (1A) to section 5 of HWA to extend these definitions to include all the latest national definitions lodged by Parties and published on the Basel Convention website.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan) (for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources)
text: Section 30 of HWA currently provides NEA with the power to control the movement of vessels or aircraft if there are reasonable grounds for suspecting that a vessel or aircraft is carrying hazardous or other waste that is to be exported from, imported into or transited through Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On seemingly pristine ice floes near the Northwest Passage, scientists, too, have discovered plastic filaments and beads.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This treaty was acceded to by Singapore in 1996 and was implemented in 1998 by the enactment of the HWA Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The amendment to the Convention classified plastic waste more clearly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Certain annexes of the convention require prior informed consent before importing such waste can be initiated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Annex IV does not require prior consent and previously classified only non-harmful plastic without specifying whether they were immediately recyclable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, clause 4 of the Bill allows our law to directly reference the prescribed website of the Secretariat of the Basel Convention as to what is considered hazardous waste.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Previously, the Minister had to declare it so via notification on the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister explain how Singapore handles our plastic waste?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do we have the capacity and capabilities to deal with our plastic waste?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides tackling the way plastic waste is handled, we can also reduce the amount of plastic pollutants released into the environment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although it has been said that "only a miniscule amount of microplastics is discharged into the sea," would the Ministry elaborate on what are the likely sources for the microplastics found on the Singapore beaches and what will be done to reduce it?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One commonly discussed source for microplastics is microbeads.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Microbeads do not disappear even though they get flushed down the sink and out of sight.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Plastic microbeads have been banned in personal care products and cosmetics in the United States (US) and United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While plastic straws are needed by some for medical conditions, some personal care products and cosmetics have been able to substitute plastic microbeads with biodegradable microbeads or even natural alternatives.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2016, it was reported in the Straits Times that the National Parks Board (NParks) was "currently looking into assessing the status and impact of marine debris and microplastics on Singapore's marine environment” and that "NEA   monitoring international developments in legislation and domestic research on microplastics." Would the Minister kindly provide an update on the findings and whether any updated studies have been done since then to understand the impact of microplastics on Singapore’s marine environment?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even though Singapore treats our used water such that a substantial portion of microbeads and microplastics are dealt with, would it not be better if there were less plastic to deal with by reducing the use and/or release of such plastics into the water?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of merely removing plastics, we should work towards reducing them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, with less plastic in our used water, there would be less incinerated ash to be disposed of.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourthly, there will be less microplastics potentially released into the environment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fifthly, we would be encouraging responsible use of plastics and would also deter the thinking that someone else will clean up the consequences of our actions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Taking into account these issues, what is the Minister's view on the question of whether we should ban the use of microplastics or microbeads in personal care products and cosmetics?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill addresses one part of the problem related to plastic waste.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the bigger question is how are we tackling this pollutant holistically?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The effect of plastic contamination is felt across national borders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Plastics and toxic-contaminated plastic in the water can enter the food chain when marine life ingest it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another possible way is via larvae of insects, such as mosquitoes, and then their being eaten by other creatures in the food chain and so on.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Research combining the results of more than 50 studies globally have estimated that an individual ingests about one credit card worth of plastic each week.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As much of our food is imported from overseas, how does the Ministry monitor the level of plastic pollutant in our food and its impact?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is there a level beyond which the plastic pollution in the food is unacceptable?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In other words, how is Singapore working towards food security and less dependency on other countries specifically in relation to seafood and other food products from the marine environment and ensuring the plastic contaminants in such food remains low or negligible?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How has Singapore contributed to innovative solutions to clean up the ocean?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is Singapore doing to encourage a global push to adopt a good plastic waste management system that reduces plastic pollution?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This indirectly contributes to Singapore's food security if our food sources are threatened by other countries’ plastic pollution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Looking at the facts, plastic pollution is a problem that we need to address.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Basel amendments are part of the global efforts to combat pollution from plastic waste, one of the biggest environmental problems our world faces due to its sheer quantity as well as the durability of plastics.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The vast amounts of plastic waste polluting water and land ecosystems are not only threatening to us and other life forms on our planet, but also to future generations.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most of this waste was exported for recycling.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Other categories of plastic waste will have to be approved by the destination countries before we can export them.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, even as we today sharpen our policies regarding the import and export of plastic waste, I would like to ask the Minister for more details of how we ourselves are disposing of our own plastic wastes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, for those plastics which are not recycled, how much is burnt and how much is buried?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, is the capacity of our landfills sufficient to meet the growing amounts of plastic waste that are generated?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, for recycled plastics, how much is processed here and how much are we actually exporting?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Fourth, are we looking to step up our capability and capacity for recycling our own plastic waste?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Fifth, how developed is the plastic waste recycling infrastructure in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sixth, will there be resources to support the research and development of plastic waste treatment here?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Seventh, as the hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza has just asked, what is the treatment for special categories, such as microplastics?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ultimately, we must reduce the use of "short-term" plastics to cut down on plastic waste, such as minimising the use of single-use plastics, particularly in non-critical areas, perhaps versus critical niches, such as in healthcare settings where it may be more difficult to replace.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Take our food and beverage (F&B) sector, for example.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am surprised that in some hawker centres and food courts, even for customers dining onsite, disposable ware is still being used.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The reasons, of course, include costs, convenience and, perhaps, hygiene.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is often not factored in is the cost we all pay for the long-term damage on our environment.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I appeal to the Ministry to work more closely with F&B providers to come up with a viable and sustainable, nationwide solution.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Due to higher costs and manpower constraints, if left to the free forces of the market, food and drinks sellers and establishments will actually have very little incentive to opt for durable, washable utensils or participate in the use and collection of reusable wares for customers who do takeaways.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also hope the Ministry would take firmer, which may perhaps be unpopular, steps to ban or severely restrict the use of certain types of single-use plastics, and the most common example would be straws.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a small nation which imports most goods, our ability to negotiate with global manufacturers for more sustainable packaging may be limited.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Nevertheless, we should still make brave attempts, persevere and work with neighbouring countries to exert pressure on big multinationals to repackage their products in environment-friendly materials.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The question at the top of most people's minds would also be what would this impact be on our economy and our business competitiveness.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would imagine that, in general, costs for some sectors would increase but I am sure that other sectors could benefit from this shift towards more environmentally-responsible practices.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could the Minister share with us his assessment of the economic impact from these amendments?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could there be assistance schemes to help affected companies during the transition phase?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How about the impact on our economy from the Ministry’s other initiatives to nudge companies to adopt environmentally-responsible practices as well as various measures towards a "zero waste" nation?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is in line with Singapore’s commitment to being a responsible global citizen, especially in environmental sustainability.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, in light of recent events, there are four issues relating to the transport of hazardous waste, including plastic waste, which I would like to address.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, I would like to ask the Minister on our compliance with our obligations under the Basel Convention so that we can evaluate our progress with the handling of hazardous waste.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: What is the current status of Singapore’s Basel Convention obligations?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: How many permits are issued for import, export and transit respectively?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: What are the destination countries where our waste goes to?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It appears difficult to know what happens to the trash afterwards.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: How do we know they are recycled or dumped properly?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A 2018 Business Times news article reported that "much of the plastic that is logged as recycled is shipped overseas – to China, Malaysia, Vietnam and Indonesia – where, if it cannot eventually be properly sorted and processed, it is incinerated or tipped into the sea." Mr Deputy Speaker, can the Minister please enlighten the House on the measures that Singapore implements to ensure that hazardous waste, per the Basel Convention, which leaves Singapore are treated to internationally-recognised standards at their destination?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, I urge the Minister to consider implementing more stringent measures to stop the illegal traffic of waste from Singapore to other countries in the region.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Treating other countries as a dumping ground without consideration for the necessary health and safety measures would be doing a great disservice to our neighbours.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There have been reported cases of illegal traffic of waste linked to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Virogreen, a Singapore-registered company, was reported by Eco-Business in March 2019 as being implicated in an "e-waste smuggling ring" in Thailand.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It reportedly exported goods labelled as "second-hand electronic appliances" from Singapore to Thailand.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In Thailand, however, it was disposed of as waste.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The waste management plants which received the e-waste salvaged the precious metals and disposed of the rest.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is not known how they salvaged the metal, or how the rest of the e-waste was disposed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, the fact that Virogreen was able to get away with declaring e-waste as functional second-hand goods is deeply concerning.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In October 2019, Reuters reported that two Singaporeans imported 87 containers of plastic scrap without the correct permits.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They are said to be a director and a commissioner of an Indonesian company respectively.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To make matters worse, the plastic scrap was reportedly contaminated with "hazardous items, such as printed circuit boards, used remote controls and used batteries", all of which could pose health hazards.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These two cases have placed a black mark on Singapore's reputation as a responsible global citizen.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has been regarding adherence to international environmental standards as a focus of Singapore's much-lauded environmental governance, and rightly so.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must ensure that Singaporean directors and Singapore-registered companies are not infringing waste regulations in the region and globally.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Increasing profit margins or reducing costs cannot be at the expense of our shared environment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans and Singapore companies, as ambassadors for Singapore, should uphold the same standards wherever they go.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is the same reason why Singapore prosecutes cases of corruption involving Singapore-registered companies under the Prevention of Corruption Act, regardless of where they happen.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As such, I would like to ask the Minister, what measures are in place to ensure that hazardous wastes are not exported under the guise of "second-hand" goods?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: What are the enforcement measures that can be used against Singaporeans and Singapore-registered entities who facilitate the contravention of the Basel Convention overseas?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Are there any plans to create extraterritorial offences, such as those found in the Prevention of Corruption Act, to allow the prosecution of Singaporeans and Singapore-registered entities?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If not, I would strongly urge the Minister to consider doing so.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to seek the Minister's clarification on the Ban Amendment to the Basel Convention.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Ban Amendment prohibits the world's wealthiest countries – the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), European Union (EU) member states, Liechtenstein – from exporting hazardous waste to non-OECD countries and forces them to internalise the costs of their own pollution.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The ban addresses the challenges faced by developing countries in controlling the flood of hazardous waste imports, which strain their infrastructure and harm the environment and local communities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister please clarify on the following: (a) Are there reasons why Singapore has not ratified the Basel Ban Amendment?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: (b) Are there any entities in Singapore which import hazardous waste, per the Basel Convention, for treatment here?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Last but not least, is there a regional role that Singapore can play in waste recycling, given that our neighbours, such as Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines, are sending back plastic waste to their places of origin?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Could implementing a circular economy mitigate our and the region’s needs with the benefits of economies of scale?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This would require manufacturers to transition from manufacturing virgin plastics to harvesting and reusing recycled plastics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Countries that bulk-import such waste bear much of the environmental and social costs, especially if they cannot manage the waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of these countries are our close neighbours in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Aligning our laws to the changes in the Basel Convention is one of the ways that Singapore can help alleviate plastic pollution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am encouraged by the amendments, which not only fulfil our international obligations but show our commitment to work with the international community to address pertinent global problems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under the new rules, countries will have to consent to importing plastic waste from exporters that are contaminated or that are difficult to recycle.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many countries have already announced plans to ban or limit their import of plastic waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such countries include China, which will ban all plastic waste imports by 2020 and other countries that take in our plastic waste, such as Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Already, Singapore incinerates some of our recyclable waste because of our limited recycling capacity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if the Ministry has reviewed its projection of the Semakau landfill's lifespan?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, can the Minister share its updated figure on the lifespan of the Semakau landfill?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If it has not done so, would the Ministry consider undertaking such a review?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify what percentage of plastic waste sent for recycling in 2019 ends up being recycled versus that which is incinerated?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the amendment means that Singapore would need to boost its local plastic recycling capacity even more urgently.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Encouragingly, NEA said last year that it is planning to build up the country’s mechanical recycling capability for used plastics and explore options for chemical recycling.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How much does the Ministry plan to invest into building up Singapore's plastic recycling capabilities?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, with Singapore's current recycling capacity, up to what percentage of our plastic waste and our overall waste, can be recycled locally respectively?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify what percentage of plastic waste we plan to recycle locally by 2035 and include a breakdown of that timeline?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, under the amended Convention, plastic that is clean, sorted and uncontaminated can be freely traded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, contamination is a key reason why we recycle only 4% of our plastic waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In recent years, MEWR and NEA have attempted to address the problem by fitting houses with a separate recycling chute and improving the information labels on blue recycling bins.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry share data on the effectiveness of these efforts to combat plastic waste contamination?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the data is not yet available, when will it be and will the Ministry publish it once it is available?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have all seen reports from neighbouring countries that have discovered toxic wastes illegally exported to their countries.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our compliance with the Basel Amendments aims to put a stop to such irresponsible practices.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Going forward, only approved categories of plastic waste can be traded without restriction, while particular categories can only be exported with the permission of the importing countries.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For Singapore and most countries, plastic waste is the biggest category of waste.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unfortunately, the amount we generate is increasing year by year.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Four percent is really pathetic and we should make much more effort to reduce the amount of plastic we use, particularly in consumable products.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many Singaporeans are supportive of the Government's efforts to be environmentally responsible but the reality is that so many of our items are packaged in plastics.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Consumers are in a bind because we do not have much of a choice.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What can we do if your shampoo or beverage comes in a plastic bottle?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important that we go upstream for solutions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The responsibility is on the manufacturers to pack their products in sustainable materials.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How should we encourage the manufacturers to improve on their products so that potential issues and concerns are addressed from the production stage to ensure that they are environmentally-friendly?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, the Ministry can consider using both the carrot and the stick to bring about improvements.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, we could impose environmental levies on products packaged in plastics and providing incentives for other materials better for our environment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, we should also introduce stronger measures to make sure that our people do their part to cut down on wastage, be responsible in recycling correctly and avoid polluting our environment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Reducing, recycling and caring for our environment should be a mindset inculcated through our education system as well as consistent public education and outreach.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These efforts should be ongoing even when it becomes part of our Singapore culture so that our younger generations will continue to uphold this value.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For higher effectiveness, I would like to request that the Ministry consider deploying more resources to its enforcement units.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I will now address the four broad areas brought up.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, the measures Singapore undertakes to meet our obligations under the Basel Convention.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Second, the effects of the amendments on the industry.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Third, our plans to develop our local recycling industry, particularly relating to plastics.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Fourth, our plans to reduce excessive consumption of plastics and to close the plastic loop.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms Anthea Ong asked about our progress in implementing the Basel Convention.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In 2018, NEA issued 36 import permits, 50 export permits and 70 transit permits.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The main destinations for Basel exports were Korea, Japan, France and Thailand, with most of these shipments containing e-waste intended for recycling.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms Anthea Ong also asked how we ensure hazardous waste exported under the Basel Convention is properly treated.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is covered under the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure, which is well-established under the Basel Convention.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: When companies apply to NEA for a Basel export permit, they are required to provide information on the treatment facility which the shipment is destined for.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This information is forwarded to the relevant authorities in the State of Import.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will not issue a Basel export permit to the company until the State of Import evaluates the proposal and consents to accept the shipment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We take our obligations under the Basel Convention seriously and have taken action against companies for violations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Individuals who commit such offences can be fined up to $100,000, or imprisoned for up to two years, or both.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA works closely with Singapore Customs and the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) to enforce these regulations at our checkpoints.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also enjoy a close working relationship with international counterparts and cooperate with them to investigate any suspected illegal export of waste from Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA had, in fact, investigated the case of Virogreen, which Ms Anthea Ong raised.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In this instance, the company had correctly declared the contents of the shipment as e-waste for recycling.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The PIC procedure had been followed and NEA had received consent from the relevant authority in Thailand for the import.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These clarifications were carried in the same Eco-Business article.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Similarly, in the case reported by Reuters, which Ms Anthea Ong cited, none of the containers had been exported from or transited through Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: No Singapore companies had contravened the Basel Convention in any way and the two Singaporeans had not violated HWA.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The case is currently under investigation by the Indonesian authorities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There are currently no plans to introduce extraterritorial offences in HWA.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Basel Convention has nearly universal membership with 187 Parties and all our neighbouring countries are members.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Singaporeans or Singapore-registered entities who contravene the Basel Convention can be prosecuted in their country of offence.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Louis Ng and Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked about the impact of the amendments on our companies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA had consulted the industry prior to the introduction of these amendments.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our companies understood the need for the new measures and for Singapore to comply with our international obligations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We do not expect these amendments to disrupt the operations of our plastic recyclers and traders.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There will not be additional regulations on the movement of most clean and homogenous plastic recyclables as these are not subjected to PIC under the Basel Convention.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mixed plastic recyclables can also continue to be exported, as long as PIC is obtained from the State of Import.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To help companies comply with the requirements, NEA will guide companies through the Basel permit application procedures, particularly in the initial period after the new regulations come into effect.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, we hope that the local recycling industry will benefit from economic opportunities as clearer regulations on the flow of recyclables develop.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will facilitate the legitimate flow of recyclables and open up new markets for our local companies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Ms Anthea Ong have pointed out, there are opportunities to promote a regional circular economy, in line with the vision of our Zero Waste Masterplan.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Plastic waste in Singapore is either recycled or incinerated.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: All general waste and recyclables must be collected by licensed collectors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Plastic recyclables that are segregated at source is sorted and sent for recycling either locally or overseas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: On the other hand, plastic waste which is not source-segregated for recycling is incinerated with other general waste at our Waste-to-Energy plants.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Of this, 7% was recycled locally, while the rest was sorted and exported for recycling.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The plastics that are recycled are mainly post-industrial plastics that are clean and homogenous, or recyclables from households that have been sorted and baled at our Material Recovery Facilities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As we can see, packaging waste, including plastics, is generated in large quantities with a low recycling rate.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Mr Louis Ng has highlighted, we hope to further build up our local recycling capabilities to better extract resources from plastic waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, I would like to clarify that we are doing this not because we contribute to the global ocean plastics problem but because we want to reduce the amount of plastics that we incinerate.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Singapore does not contribute in any significant way to the ocean plastics problem.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We do not landfill our plastic waste but incinerate them at our Waste-to-Energy plants.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Most of Singapore is a water catchment, meaning that our waterways are dammed up and plastics are removed from the waterways before they reach our reservoirs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have been building up our waste management resilience, which is in line with the global movement towards proper treatment and management of waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As a small country, in the face of carbon and resource constraints, we also want to enhance Singapore's resource resilience by reusing resources for as long as possible.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hence, our vision is to close the plastic waste loop locally where feasible and allow our plastic wastes to be recovered and converted into useful resources again.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: At the same time, investing in new recycling technology and developing the industry will create economic opportunities and good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, McKinsey estimates a potential fourfold increase in plastics reuse and recycling by 2030, worth an estimated US$60 billion.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are studying both mechanical and chemical recycling options.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mechanical recycling uses well-established technology to turn waste plastics into plastic pellets.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We already have mechanical recycling plants in Singapore which treat our industrial plastic waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These are operated by companies, such as A~Star Plastics, Plaspulp Union and Ravago.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Waste plastics that are not suitable for mechanical recycling, such as used plastic bags, can be recycled into chemical feedstock through chemical recycling.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will share more on our plans to close the plastics loop at the upcoming Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Based on our consultations with industry players, the main impediments to greater recycling locally are the lack of economies of scale and low global demand.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will require further consultations with the local industry and economic agencies to determine the appropriate industry size and structure to suit the Singapore market.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our intent to build up local recycling capability is also a key reason why Singapore has not ratified the Ban Amendment, which Ms Anthea Ong asked about.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Amendment was first introduced in 1995 to protect developing countries from the ill-effects of hazardous waste exported by developed countries.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Amendment bans all exports from developed to developing countries, hence its name.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We believe that the legitimate movement of useful waste material does not just present economic opportunities for our companies, but allows Singapore to play our part in the safe handling of hazardous material in the region.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, e-waste recycling companies in Singapore import e-waste from countries, such as Japan, South Korea and New Zealand, and treat them at our licensed facilities in an environmentally-sound manner.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This would be curtailed if we ratified the Ban Amendment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, many OECD countries have not ratified the Ban Amendment yet, including countries with strong recycling industries, such as Japan and South Korea.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are also investing in research and development (R&D) to develop local recycling solutions, as Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Mr Louis Ng spoke about.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, it has funded a research project that is studying how plastic-embedded multi-layer films, such as potato chip packaging, can be recycled.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This involves developing a chemical recycling method that can separate and individually recycle the different layers from the multi-layer film.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Gan Thiam Poh have highlighted, it is key to reduce the generation of plastic waste in the first place.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This year, new regulations on the mandatory reporting of packaging data and the Reduce, Reuse and Recycle (3R) plans for packaging will take effect.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Mr Gan Thiam Poh highlighted, such regulations will force companies to be more conscious of the amount of packaging used in their products and encourage them to identify ways to optimise packaging.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The EPR framework ensures that producers are responsible for the collection and recycling of the materials they use to package their products.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will send economic signals to companies to take into account the cost of environmental externalities of their products.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will also encourage the redesigning of products so that less materials are used or the products can be more easily recycled.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, tackling the consumption of plastics cannot be done by the Government alone.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are working closely with various stakeholders to reduce our consumption of disposables, including plastics.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, NEA's "Say YES to Waste Less" campaign has partnered 1,600 premises to encourage consumers to reduce the use of disposables.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also want to partner Singaporeans to co-create other solutions to reduce the excessive consumption of plastics.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will announce further details on this later this year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Mr Christopher de Souza raised the issue of microplastics and microbeads.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have in place comprehensive measures to address microplastics.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, SFA routinely takes samples of locally available food, including seafood, for testing to ensure compliance with our food safety standards.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: At the same time, we recognise that the World Health Organization, European Food Safety Authority and Food Agriculture Organisation have assessed that microplastics either posed a low risk to human health, or that more scientific evidence was required to assess the impact of ingesting plastic in food.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Public Utilities Board (PUB) also treats all used water at our water reclamation plants to internationally recognised discharge standards using the latest technology.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: While we have no plans to ban microbeads in cosmetics, we encourage businesses to reduce the use of microbeads in their products.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I am heartened that multinational corporations, such as Johnson & Johnson and Unilever, as well as our own local retailers, like Guardian Singapore and Watsons, have phased out microbeads in their products.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to monitor international developments on microplastics, including microbeads in cosmetics.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Plastic waste is a waste stream of concern for us, and we are tackling it through regulations under the Resource Sustainability Act, as well as other plans to reduce plastic consumption and promote plastics recycling under the Zero Waste Masterplan.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, as a responsible member of the international community, Singapore remains committed to upholding our obligations under the Basel Convention.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Bill will also allow for a more effective administration and enforcement of the Convention.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The amendments to the Basel Convention will provide greater clarity on plastic waste standards and better regulate its transboundary movement.
